What To Do: Decide, together with the client, whether we forecast at the SKU level, product-category level, or total demand — and whether we do it daily, weekly, or monthly.
Why It Matters: This single decision shapes every model and dataset that follows. Getting it wrong means redoing feature engineering and modeling later. Weekly granularity is our working recommendation given the seasonality involved.
Deliverable: A one-page written decision (forecasting unit + granularity) confirmed with the client.

What To Do: Determine how many weeks/months ahead the client needs forecasts, based on their procurement and shipping lead times.
Why It Matters: The horizon determines which models are even viable and how we split data for training vs. testing.
Deliverable: Documented forecast horizon (e.g., '10 weeks ahead') agreed with the client.

What To Do: Create a simple model that predicts demand for a given week as equal to demand in the same week last year. No machine learning involved — just a lookup.
Why It Matters: This is our most important reference point because it already captures the seasonal pattern. Every future model must beat this to be worth using.
Deliverable: A working seasonal-naive forecast script/notebook and its accuracy numbers.
Tool / Service (free): pandas / PySpark on serverless or single-node cluster
Cost Control Note: Use serverless SQL/compute or a small single-node cluster with auto-termination enabled.

What To Do: Create a second, simpler baseline using a moving average or exponential smoothing over recent weeks.
Why It Matters: Gives us a second, smoother point of comparison — useful for sanity-checking whether the seasonal naive model above is actually adding value.
Deliverable: A working moving-average/exponential-smoothing notebook and its accuracy numbers.
Tool / Service (free): pandas / PySpark + statsmodels (exp. smoothing) — open source
Cost Control Note: Same compute as 1.3; no extra service.

What To Do: Split the 2020–2026 historical data by time (e.g., train 2020-2024, validate 2025, hold out 2026) instead of randomly shuffling rows.
Why It Matters: Random shuffling would leak future information into training and make our accuracy numbers falsely optimistic — a common time-series mistake we must avoid.
Deliverable: A documented, reusable split definition (date ranges for train/validation/test).

What To Do: Instead of testing on just one holdout period, repeatedly move the 'cutoff date' forward in time and re-test, so we see performance across several different periods.
Why It Matters: One holdout year could be misleading if it happened to include an unusual event (e.g., a supply shock). Testing across multiple rolling windows gives a much more trustworthy performance estimate.
Deliverable: A reusable walk-forward validation function/notebook that any model can be plugged into.
Cost Control Note: Repeated re-fits add compute time — keep on serverless/auto-terminating compute, not an always-on cluster.

What To Do: Set up the three metrics we'll use for every model going forward: MAPE (percentage error), RMSE (penalizes big misses), and Bias (systematic over/under-forecasting). Also create a special 'peak season only' version of each metric.
Why It Matters: The client cares more about not running out of stock during peak season than about being perfectly accurate the rest of the year — so we need a metric that reflects that priority, not just an overall average.
Deliverable: A metrics calculation script producing MAPE, RMSE, and Bias, both overall and for the peak-season weeks specifically.

Task Name: Log the baseline as 'Experiment 0' in MLflow
What To Do: Record the seasonal naive and moving-average baseline results (from 1.3/1.4) as the very first MLflow experiment, so every future model can be compared against it.
Why It Matters: This becomes our permanent 'floor' — no future model should be adopted unless it clearly beats this recorded baseline.
Deliverable: An MLflow experiment named '00_baseline' containing both baseline runs with their metrics logged.
Cost Control Note: No cost — MLflow has no separate billing on the workspace.

Task Name: Build the feature backlog with causal hypotheses
What To Do: Create a shared list of candidate features (calendar, holidays, weather, economic, marketing, internal/inventory) and write a one-sentence hypothesis for why each one should affect demand.
Why It Matters: Writing the hypothesis first stops us from adding features just because they happen to correlate — we want features we can explain to the client, not black-box coincidences.
Deliverable: A shared feature backlog document/spreadsheet with one row per candidate feature and its hypothesis.

What To Do: Add features like month, week-of-year, and 'days until summer season' to the baseline model.
Why It Matters: This is the lowest-risk, highest-certainty feature group given how seasonal these products are — a natural first step.
Deliverable: An MLflow run named 'baseline+calendar' with updated metrics and a written note on whether it beat the baseline.

What To Do: Add flags for public holidays and long weekends to the model from step 2.2.
Why It Matters: Boating and nautical-product purchases likely cluster around holidays and long weekends, so this tests a specific, well-understood driver.
Deliverable: An MLflow run named 'baseline+calendar+holidays' with updated metrics and a short write-up of the impact.

What To Do: Source and add weather data (temperature, precipitation, wind/marine conditions) to the model.
Why It Matters: Bad weather likely suppresses boating-related purchases — but weather may also just be redundant with the season/month feature already in the model, so we need to test it carefully.
Deliverable: An MLflow run with weather features added, plus a specific check for whether weather adds value beyond calendar features alone (see task 2.9).
Cost Control Note: Weather data must come from an external free-tier API — confirm that provider's free request limits before relying on it in production.

What To Do: Source and add macroeconomic indicators such as consumer confidence index, fuel prices, and interest rates.
Why It Matters: Nautical products are discretionary/leisure purchases, so they may be sensitive to the broader economy — this tests that hypothesis.
Deliverable: An MLflow run with economic features added and a written note on the performance impact.
Cost Control Note: Same caution as 2.4: verify the external economic-data source's free usage limits.

What To Do: Add data on discount events and marketing campaign spend to the model, while explicitly checking whether these features are only showing up as predictive because promotions are timed to already-expected demand (reverse causality).
Why It Matters: This feature carries a real risk of looking helpful for the wrong reason. We need to be careful it's not just 'predicting' demand that the marketing team already knew was coming.
Deliverable: An MLflow run with promotion features added, plus a written note addressing the reverse-causality risk specifically.

Task Name: Add internal features & correct for censored demand
What To Do: Add inventory-on-hand, stockout history, and price-change data. First, check whether 'units sold' in the historical data was ever capped by 'units in stock' (i.e., we couldn't sell what we didn't have) and correct for this before using it.
Why It Matters: If past stockouts suppressed recorded sales, our 'demand' numbers for those periods understate true demand. Feeding that directly into the model would teach it to under-forecast — the opposite of what the client needs.
Deliverable: A documented correction method for censored demand periods, plus an MLflow run with internal features added.

Task Name: Investigate and handle the 2020–2021 COVID anomaly
What To Do: Analyze whether the 2020-2021 period shows unusually high or low demand compared to the surrounding years, and decide whether to down-weight, exclude, or flag those years in training.
Why It Matters: If left untreated, the model may learn patterns from an unrepeatable, one-time shock and apply them incorrectly to future forecasts.
Deliverable: A written recommendation (with supporting charts) on how 2020-2021 data should be treated, agreed upon by the team.

Task Name: Check multicollinearity between weather and calendar features
What To Do: Statistically test whether the weather features (task 2.4) are actually adding new information, or whether they're just duplicating what month/season already tells the model.
Why It Matters: Redundant features add complexity and can make the model harder to interpret without improving accuracy — worth confirming before finalizing the feature set.
Deliverable: A short written analysis stating whether weather features should be kept, simplified, or dropped.

What To Do: Review all feature experiments (2.2–2.9), confirm which features produced meaningful, explainable improvements (e.g., >2% MAPE gain), and lock in the final feature list for modeling.
Why It Matters: Once we stop finding meaningful gains, continuing to add features just adds complexity and risk of overfitting — this step marks the transition into model comparison.
Deliverable: A finalized, documented feature list (the 'frozen' feature set) that every model in Phase 3 will use.

What To Do: Train a linear regression model using the frozen feature set, including seasonal/trend terms.
Why It Matters: This is our most interpretable model — useful for explaining forecasts to the client in plain terms, even if it isn't the final production model.
Deliverable: An MLflow run with the linear regression model, its metrics, and a summary of which features matter most.

What To Do: Train a Random Forest model on the same frozen feature set.
Why It Matters: Random Forest captures non-linear patterns and feature interactions automatically, but tends to struggle predicting values higher than anything seen historically — worth watching if 2026 demand sets new records.
Deliverable: An MLflow run with the Random Forest model, its metrics, and feature importance results.

What To Do: Train an XGBoost model on the frozen feature set, then tune its settings (learning rate, tree depth, regularization) using an automated search tool (e.g., Hyperopt) tracked in MLflow.
Why It Matters: XGBoost is typically the strongest performer on this type of data and is our leading candidate for the production model — worth the extra tuning effort.
Deliverable: An MLflow run (or set of runs) showing the tuning process and the best XGBoost model with its metrics.
Cost Control Note: Hyperparameter search runs many trials — cap trial count and keep on auto-terminating compute; no GPU cluster needed for this data size.

What To Do: Train a Prophet model, which is purpose-built for seasonal, holiday-driven time series like this one.
Why It Matters: Prophet is a strong natural fit given how seasonal these products are, and is a good candidate to combine with XGBoost later.
Deliverable: An MLflow run with the Prophet model, its metrics, and a plot of its trend/seasonality decomposition.

What To Do: Train a SARIMA model as an additional statistical benchmark, using the product's own historical values and seasonal patterns.
Why It Matters: This isn't expected to be our top performer given how feature-rich our data is, but it's a useful, well-established benchmark to compare against.
Deliverable: An MLflow run with the SARIMA model and its metrics.

What To Do: If Prophet and XGBoost make different kinds of errors (check this first), combine their forecasts (e.g., a weighted average) into a single ensemble prediction.
Why It Matters: Combining two models that are wrong in different ways often produces a more accurate and more robust forecast than either model alone.
Deliverable: An MLflow run with the ensemble model and its metrics, plus a note on why/whether it improved on the individual models.

Task Name: Run standardized evaluation across all models
What To Do: Score every model (3.1–3.6) using the exact same rolling-origin validation windows and the same metrics (MAPE, RMSE, Bias), including the peak-season-only slice.
Why It Matters: This ensures we're comparing all models fairly, on equal terms, and specifically checking who performs best when it matters most — during peak season.
Deliverable: A single comparison table/report showing all models side-by-side on every metric and time window.

What To Do: As a team, review the comparison report from 3.7 and select the best model (or ensemble) to move forward as the production 'Champion'.
Why It Matters: This is a key decision checkpoint — it should be a team discussion, not just 'pick whatever has the lowest number,' since peak-season reliability matters more than average accuracy.
Deliverable: A written decision record naming the champion model and the reasoning behind the choice.

What To Do: Create the four MLflow experiments we'll use throughout the project: 00_baseline, 01_feature_iteration, 02_model_comparison, 03_final_tuning.
Why It Matters: Organizing experiments this way from the start keeps every run traceable and makes it easy for anyone on the team (or the client) to see the project's history later.
Deliverable: Four MLflow experiments created and ready to receive runs, with a naming convention documented for the team.

Task Name: Set up Delta Lake tables for raw & feature data
What To Do: Load the historical sales data (and later, engineered features) into versioned Delta Lake tables in Databricks.
Why It Matters: Delta Lake's version history lets us trace any model back to the exact snapshot of data it was trained on — important for debugging and for client trust.
Deliverable: Delta tables set up for raw sales data and feature data, accessible to the whole team.

What To Do: Turn the feature engineering steps from Phase 2 into a reusable, versioned notebook or pipeline (rather than one-off scripts), so it can be re-run consistently as new data arrives.
Why It Matters: A reusable pipeline avoids duplicated work and prevents subtle differences between how features were computed during training vs. later in production.
Deliverable: A versioned feature engineering notebook/pipeline that reproduces the frozen feature set from task 2.10.

What To Do: If we expect to reuse the same features across multiple SKU-level models, register them in the Databricks Feature Store instead of recomputing them each time.
Why It Matters: This prevents 'training/serving skew' — a common bug where features are computed slightly differently at training time vs. prediction time.
Deliverable: Feature Store tables set up (or a documented decision that this isn't needed yet).
Cost Control Note: Included with a Unity-Catalog-enabled workspace at no extra service cost; optional for this project's scale.

Task Name: Orchestrate walk-forward validation with Databricks Jobs
What To Do: Automate the rolling-origin validation process (task 1.6) as a scheduled/repeatable Databricks Job, instead of running it manually each time.
Why It Matters: Automation reduces manual error and lets the team re-validate models quickly whenever new data or features are added.
Deliverable: A working Databricks Job that runs the full validation pipeline on demand or on a schedule.
Cost Control Note: Job clusters bill for runtime — use small/serverless job clusters with auto-termination and schedule no more frequently than needed.

Task Name: Configure MLflow Model Registry & promotion gates
What To Do: Set up the Model Registry so models can move through 'Staging' and 'Production' stages, with a clear rule that a new model can only be promoted if it beats the current Champion on peak-season performance specifically.
Why It Matters: This creates a safe, auditable process for updating the production model over time, instead of ad-hoc swaps.
Deliverable: A configured Model Registry with the baseline model registered as the first 'Champion', and documented promotion criteria.

Task Name: Build a Champion vs. Challenger comparison view
What To Do: Create a simple dashboard or report that always shows the current production model side-by-side with any new candidate model being tested.
Why It Matters: This becomes our ongoing discipline for evaluating new ideas fairly against what's already live, rather than comparing against ever-shifting baselines.
Deliverable: A working dashboard/report (e.g., in Databricks SQL or a notebook) showing Champion vs. Challenger metrics.
Cost Control Note: No cost within the existing workspace.

What To Do: Create a scheduled job that compares the live model's forecasts against actual sales as they come in, and logs the ongoing accuracy.
Why It Matters: Model accuracy naturally degrades over time as the market changes (new products, shifting trends) — we need to catch this early rather than find out from the client.
Deliverable: A scheduled monitoring job producing regular accuracy reports comparing forecasts to actuals.
Cost Control Note: Same caution as 4.5 — keep the monitoring job's schedule and cluster size minimal.

What To Do: Agree on and document a specific rule for when the model should be retrained — e.g., if rolling MAPE degrades beyond a set threshold over a set number of weeks — rather than retraining on an arbitrary calendar schedule.
Why It Matters: A clear, objective trigger avoids both 'retraining too often for no reason' and 'waiting too long while the model quietly gets worse.'
Deliverable: A written retraining policy with specific thresholds, agreed upon by the team.

What To Do: Roll up the champion model's store/product forecasts to each distribution center's service area and compute period-over-period growth.
Why It Matters: This directly answers the client's question on demand growth at distribution centers over the 3-month forecast period.
Deliverable: A Delta table of DC-level forecasted demand and growth rate for the 3-month horizon.

Task Name: Identify highest-growth DC & point of sale
What To Do: Rank distribution centers and points of sale by forecasted demand growth and visualize the top movers.
Why It Matters: Pinpoints exactly where the business should focus capacity/inventory planning first.
Deliverable: A ranked chart/table of DCs and points of sale by forecasted growth.
Tool / Service (free): PySpark/pandas + matplotlib or Databricks SQL Dashboard

What To Do: Cluster high-growth, under-served store locations (e.g., k-means or geospatial density) to test whether new DC locations are justified, and if so, propose candidate sites.
Why It Matters: Directly answers the client's question on whether new distribution centers should be created, and where.
Deliverable: A written recommendation with supporting maps/clusters naming candidate DC locations (or concluding none are needed).
Cost Control Note: No cost; runs on existing compute.

What To Do: Package charts, metrics tables, and recommendations answering all four client questions (a-d) into a shared notebook or dashboard for the team to finalize.
Why It Matters: Gives the team a single, presentable source of truth to hand back to the client.
Deliverable: A consolidated notebook/dashboard covering forecast, seasonality, model comparison, DC growth, and new-DC recommendation.
